title: L'Auberge Espagnole
full_review:
"L'Auberge Espagnole" (Fox Searchlight) is a patchwork comedy about eight exchange students -- each from a different European country -- exploring the shifting tectonics of modern multicultural relationships while sharing an apartment in sunny Spain.

Though the Benetton-poster faces and kinetic style chosen by director Cedric Klapisch are fresh, the film's message -- embrace a bohemian libertinism or suffer the suffocating consequences -- is anything but novel.

Using the vibrant allure of Barcelona as a backdrop, the film follows the fate of Xavier (Romain Duris), a 25-year-old economics grad student from Paris who comes to Spain as part of an inter-European exchange program named Erasmus, after the globe-trotting Renaissance scholar. Xavier, who wants to be a writer, is heartsick about leaving behind his French-tart girlfriend, Martine (Audrey Tautou), to study abroad for a year -- a move prompted by his practical father which will lead to a job offer dealing with the burgeoning Iberian market.

Xavier arrives, unable to speak the language -- a stranger to himself in a city full of strangers. Searching for a place to stay, he falls in with a couple of fellow Frenchies, who also recently arrived from Paris: Jean Michel (Xavier De Guillebon), a bombastic neurologist, and his sultry -- albeit repressed -- wife, Anne-Sophie (Judith Godreche), whom he leaves in Xavier's charge.

Xavier scours the city for something more permanent, stumbling across a notice advertising a crammed flat shared by a veritable NATO alliance of seven similarly aged students whose personalities are as varied as their nationalities and sexual proclivities.

The polyglot lodging becomes a "L'Auberge Espagnole" -- translated literally, meaning "Spanish Inn" but in French slang also connotes a place where cultures mix -- setting the stage for predictable bonding-by-booze scenarios.

Along the way, Xavier finds himself entangled in a "menage a trois" of deception involving Martine, Anne-Sophie and one of his roommates, Isabelle (Cecile De France), a libidinous lesbian from whom Xavier receives a tutorial in international relations.

The filmmaker uses attractive young faces to peddle unattractive old ideas. Much of the film's objectionable content stems from a dangerous philosophical attitude posited by the filmmaker: "It seemed that as I made the movie, I learned with Xavier that following the most unconscious desires and mixed up impulses is a good way to grow up and experience life with freedom. In the end, it became a movie, not only about youth and travel and diversity, but about finding that freedom."

Within the context of this quote, freedom -- in the sense of moral autonomy -- justifies all the characters' actions. Once unfettered freedom becomes the film's prime directive, anything is permissible; carte blanche is granted to indulge in "the most unconscious desires and mixed-up impulses" -- even if that includes adultery. A la carte sex is de rigueur; why not? As one character states, "It's just sex."

However, Klapisch does frown on one form of free expression. Midway through the film, Wendy (Keilly Reilly), the Brit of the bunch, gets a visit from her blowhard brother, William (Kevin Bishop), whose politically incorrect babbling offends some of the roommates' ethnic sensitivities. For much of the remainder, William is treated as a pariah -- true to the hypocrisy of relativism, his tongue is not afforded the same liberties as their genitals. Of course, William is redeemed in the end when he lies to Wendy's boyfriend who shows up unexpectedly from England, in order to cover up for her while she's in bed with another guy.

Against the youthful cast's vitality, the film pits members of the older generation, composed primarily of stuffy cogs in the corporate machine, such as Xavier's father, or curmudgeons, like the landlord -- who is so out of touch with their "Real World" lifestyle that he actually complains that the flat is a pigsty and that a niche once used for a statue of the Madonna is now occupied by a robot action figure. Xavier's mom does get a bit of a free pass but, hey, she's an ex-hippie.

Regrettably, inside this Euro-pudding is little more than Euro-trash.

Subtitles.

Due to its acceptance of casual sex, adulterous sexual encounters with nudity, lesbian kissing, recurring substance abuse, and much rough language and profanities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
